newsitem.title: USA: SEC eyes possible yield burning by major MD issuer.
newsitem.headline: SEC eyes possible yield burning by major MD issuer.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into whether "yield burning" occurred in a $435.6 million bond refunding deal issued by the Washington Surburban Sanitary District in January 1994, the district's investment chief said Wednesday.

Joseph Carrigan, director of investment and funding for the sanitary district, which maintains drinking water facilities for two suburban Washington D.C. counties, told Reuters that SEC has informally telephoned him about the deal, but has not subpoenaed him.
SEC's informal probe of the district, one of the nation's largest municipal bond issuers, was first uncovered by Grant's Bond Observer, which reports the story in its Feb 7 edition.

"Yield burning" refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharged issuers in the early 1990s for U.S. Treasury securities purchased in the open market and used in bond refinancing transactions. Carrigan would not comment further on the SEC's probe.

But a sanitary district source said, "They are asking questions about yield burning. I just don't know where it's going. They are trying to find out if there was yield burning involved because it's a big issue."
William Baker, and SEC assistant director for enforcement, who is helping to oversee a recent SEC crackdown on yield burning, was unavailble for comment.

Grants says the markup on the escrow for the sanitary district's January 1994 refunding appears to have been $3.68 million, or an average of roughly $12 per $1,000 bond. "Some of the markups, on zero-coupon bonds due in 2001, appear to have been $37.65, Grants says.

The financial adviser on the 1994 refunding deal was Alex. Brown & Sons. Grants says the firm also provided the escrow. Douglas Carter, manager of public finance for Alex. Brown was unavailable for comment.
